<reason>A (CON) edged an excellent, closely matched debate. Both sides obeyed format, answered Q1/Q2 with labeled A1/A2, and used grounded examples (UNCC, Algiers, windfall-interest practice) without fake authority; symmetric clipping was a wash. A turned B's own Iraq precedent in the opening, gave the only concrete freeze-to-lawful-compensation mechanism (Algiers), and directly met B's endpoint dilemma with conditioned custody, successor-state settlement, and windfall income rebuilding now. B's closing was the single best speech — "indefinite custody is confiscation without the trial" — but A's closing answered that frame head-on via reversibility and title vs. custody. The decisive residue: B's symmetry defense (no third jurisdiction will recognize mirror judgments) was shown by A to be non-responsive, since retaliatory seizure happens domestically where investors' assets already sit, and B never repaired that hole. A ends with more live, unneutralized routes; B has the better rhetoric but a thinner answer on who absorbs the systemic cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.5's mirror-court counter: B claimed recognition abroad filters bad judgments, but A pointed out the boomerang needs no recognition — seizure happens at home under domestic law. It gutted B's answer to the symmetry question and was never addressed again, while B's best counter-move (permanent taking without trial) was at least substantively engaged by A's conditioned-custody distinction.</best_rebuttal>
